name: e4
responses: Keeping a crisis contained is generally preferable because opening a second theater or domain can broaden the conflict, create escalation risks, strain resources, and make signaling and control more difficult. Accepting a local disadvantage may be costly, but it preserves the possibility of de-escalation and limits harm. A cross-domain or secondary-theater move should be considered only when necessary, proportionate, and carefully controlled—not as a routine way to relieve pressure.

Keeping the crisis contained should prevail because opening a second theater or domain risks horizontal escalation, miscalculation, and a broader conflict that may be much harder to control. Accepting some local disadvantage preserves strategic stability and allows the state to use lower-risk tools—such as diplomacy, sanctions, defensive reinforcement, and coalition support—to improve its position. A second front should be considered only under exceptionally clear conditions, not as a routine way to relieve pressure.
